periods.analysis: The Employee Engagement Index opened this cycle at 73, which is 1 point above the >=72 target and therefore green. As a baseline quarter, I am treating the result as acceptable but not self-executing; the margin above target is narrow enough that normal hiring, overtime, or supervisor turnover could erode it. The strongest early control signal came from the Finance & Administration pulse cohorts in Payroll, Procurement, and Customer Service, where managers completed the new 30-day follow-up logs in Workday for 87% of flagged comments. We also saw practical benefit from the Harborview Listens roundtables held at City Hall and the North Operations Annex, particularly on workload clarity and internal communications.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the green result by keeping the 30-day comment follow-up log mandatory for every department with five or more survey comments. I recommend adding a quarterly risk review to the HR dashboard that tracks engagement by division, vacancy rate, and overtime hours together, so we do not miss early pressure points. Continue the Harborview Listens roundtables, but rotate the next sessions to Public Works Field Services and the Permit Center to broaden coverage.

periods.analysis: The index increased from 73 to 75, a quarter-over-quarter movement of +2, and remains green against the >=72 target. That is a constructive improvement, and it appears linked to completion of the supervisor check-in pilot for 42 front-line leads and the launch of the Open Enrollment help desk at the Civic Center. I would not overstate the gain, because year-end budget work and holiday staffing can mask fatigue in smaller teams, but the control environment is improving. Comment coding showed fewer unresolved concerns in benefits navigation and more favorable feedback on direct-manager responsiveness.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the +2 improvement by converting the supervisor check-in pilot into a standard quarterly requirement for all supervisors with direct reports. HR should preserve the Open Enrollment help desk model and publish a post-enrollment issue log with owners and due dates by January 15. I also recommend setting a watch-item for high-volume teams in Utility Billing and Accounts Payable, where seasonal transaction loads can affect engagement even when the citywide score is green.

periods.analysis: The index moved from 75 to 74, a quarter-over-quarter movement of -1, while still remaining green and 2 points above the >=72 target. The decline is modest, but it is a useful control warning because it followed the post-holiday workload surge, the Munis upgrade training window, and a heavy recruitment schedule for summer programs. The new-hire cohort hired between October and December reported solid onboarding satisfaction, but several comments pointed to inconsistent cross-training in the Permit Center and Records units. In financial-risk terms, the result is healthy, but the cushion narrowed and should be actively protected.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the green status by requiring each department to document one cross-training action in the Q2 workforce plan, with HR sampling completion for control assurance. Extend the new-hire onboarding survey from 30 days to include a 90-day check, especially for cohorts in permitting, records, and seasonal recreation hiring. I recommend Finance & Administration review Munis training tickets by division and close any recurring knowledge gaps before the Q2 close process.

periods.analysis: The index declined again from 74 to 73, a quarter-over-quarter movement of -1, but remains green at 1 point above the >=72 target. This is the second consecutive small decline, so I view the status as positive but watchful rather than comfortable. The main operational pressures were predictable: budget adoption, spring permit volume on the Shoreline Corridor, and overtime in customer-facing counters during two vacancies. The Engagement Action Register shows that 19 of 23 department actions were completed, which is good execution, but the remaining open items are concentrated in higher-contact teams where delay carries retention risk.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the green result by closing the four overdue Engagement Action Register items before the end of July and reporting exceptions to the executive team. Add a targeted retention control for customer-facing teams: monthly vacancy, overtime, and engagement-comment review for Utility Billing, Permit Intake, and the Service Desk. I recommend extending the supervisor check-in standard with a short script on workload triage so managers address capacity concerns consistently.

periods.analysis: The index improved from 73 to 74, a quarter-over-quarter movement of +1, keeping the measure green and restoring a slightly larger cushion above the >=72 target. The improvement suggests the Q2 corrective controls had effect, particularly the closure of the overdue action items and the deployment of two temporary permit technicians on the H-17 counter rotation. Participation in the Harborview Listens sessions at Fire Station 6 and the Parks Maintenance Yard was stronger than expected, and the issues raised were more specific, which makes them easier to manage. I still read the result cautiously because 74 is stable but not high enough to absorb unmanaged workload shocks.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the +1 gain by keeping the temporary permit-technician coverage through the fall construction closeout period and measuring its effect on overtime. Extend the Engagement Action Register by adding a risk rating for each action, so high-impact workforce concerns cannot sit behind low-risk process improvements. HR should also repeat the Parks and Fire Station listening format in the Library and Community Development groups, where dispersed schedules can reduce visibility.

periods.analysis: The index increased from 74 to 75, a quarter-over-quarter movement of +1, and remains green, now 3 points above the >=72 target. This is the second consecutive improvement, which gives more confidence that the management actions are taking hold rather than producing a one-time response. The strongest operational evidence was completion of 96% of required supervisor check-ins and the first clean quarterly reconciliation between engagement actions and vacancy data in the HR controls workbook. Year-end workload remains a standing risk, but the city entered it with better documentation, clearer owners, and fewer unresolved employee-comment themes than last year.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the 75 result by preserving the supervisor check-in completion control at or above 95% and reviewing exceptions by department head. Extend the HR controls workbook to include internal promotion rates and training completion, because engagement risk often appears first in mobility and development data. I recommend locking the Q1 listening calendar now, before budget kickoff compresses manager availability.

periods.analysis: The index fell from 75 to 73, a quarter-over-quarter movement of -2, but remains green at 1 point above the >=72 target. The drop is material enough to warrant attention, even though it does not breach the target, because it gives back the gains achieved in late 2025. The likely drivers were first-quarter budget preparation, winter storm overtime in facilities and fleet support, and manager transitions in two administrative divisions. Control follow-up was adequate, with all departments submitting action updates, but the comment review showed renewed concern about workload predictability and communication during schedule changes.
periods.recommendations: Sustain green status by opening a 60-day workload predictability review for divisions with overtime above plan or manager turnover during Q1. Require department heads to certify that schedule-change communications are issued at least seven days in advance when operationally feasible, with exceptions logged. I recommend a focused pulse survey in April for Facilities, Fleet Administration, Budget, and Customer Service to confirm whether the -2 movement is stabilizing or continuing.

periods.analysis: The index improved from 73 to 74, a quarter-over-quarter movement of +1, and remains green against the >=72 target. This recovery is a favorable sign that the Q1 workload and communication controls helped, though the measure is still below the 75 level reached in 2025-Q4. The April pulse survey identified schedule clarity as the most actionable issue, and the follow-up use of shared crew calendars in Facilities and Fleet Administration appears to have reduced friction. From a risk perspective, Harborview remains in good position, but the narrow 2-point cushion above target requires continued discipline rather than celebration.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the +1 recovery by making shared crew calendars and seven-day schedule notices standard practice in all administrative support teams by August 31. Extend the focused pulse-survey method to any division with a quarter-over-quarter engagement decline of 2 points or more, so intervention is triggered before the index approaches yellow. I recommend maintaining the quarterly linkage of engagement, overtime, vacancy, and training data as a standing Finance & Administration control.

periods.analysis: The available engagement index is 67, five points below the 72 threshold. The source value differs from the previous commentary's 74; this carry-forward cannot establish when the decline occurred.
periods.recommendations: Confirm the survey extract with HR, then use division-level responses and schedule-clarity feedback to set manager follow-up actions.
